clinicalPearls: Proximal median nerve compression in the forearm presenting with volar forearm aching aggravated by repetitive pronation, distinguishing it from the nocturnal wrist-centred symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome.
Sensory disturbance characteristically involves the thenar eminence via the palmar cutaneous branch, which arises proximal to the wrist and is therefore spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Compression may occur at the ligament of Struthers, the lacertus fibrosus, between the two heads of pronator teres, or at the fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis.
A negative Tinel sign at the wrist with a positive provocative response over the proximal forearm supports the diagnosis.

Provocative manoeuvres attempt to localise the site: resisted pronation with the elbow extended implicates pronator teres, resisted elbow flexion with supination implicates lacertus fibrosus, and resisted long-finger flexion implicates the superficialis arch.
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography are frequently normal or non-localising, so the diagnosis remains largely clinical.
Unlike anterior interosseous syndrome, weakness is usually mild and sensory symptoms predominate, though overlap occurs when the parent median nerve is affected.
A supracondylar humeral spur with the ligament of Struthers is a rare bony cause and may be visible on radiographs.
reference.pathophysiology: The median nerve traverses several potential compression points in the proximal forearm: a supracondylar spur bridged by the ligament of Struthers, the bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus), the interval between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres, and the proximal fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis. Repetitive forceful pronation and gripping, muscular hypertrophy, anatomical anomalies, or a space-occupying lesion produce mechanical and ischaemic injury to the nerve. Because the palmar cutaneous and thenar motor branches arise at or distal to this level, both thenar sensation and, variably, thenar motor function may be affected, contrasting with the pattern seen in wrist-level entrapment.
additionalDifferentials: brachial plexopathy involving the lateral cord
cervical rib or thoracic outlet syndrome
additionalInvestigations: nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of median-innervated forearm and hand muscles
elbow and humeral radiographs to identify a supracondylar spur
high-resolution nerve ultrasound of the proximal forearm
magnetic resonance imaging of the elbow and forearm for mass lesions or muscle oedema
cervical spine imaging when radiculopathy is suspected
comparison studies of the contralateral limb
dynamic provocative examination during electrodiagnostic testing
redFlags: rapidly progressive motor weakness suggesting an alternative or compressive mass lesion
constitutional symptoms or a palpable forearm mass indicating neoplasm
bilateral or multifocal deficits suggesting a systemic or inflammatory neuropathy
acute severe pain with swelling raising concern for compartment syndrome
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with activity modification, splinting and conservative measures, and surgical decompression is generally effective when a discrete compressive structure is identified. Recovery may be slow and incomplete when diagnosis is delayed or the compression is diffuse.
pitfalls: mislabelling proximal median symptoms as carpal tunnel syndrome and performing an unhelpful wrist release
expecting confirmatory electrodiagnostic findings when studies are frequently normal
overlooking a supracondylar spur by omitting elbow radiographs
confusing the sensory-predominant picture with the pure motor deficit of anterior interosseous syndrome
references: Dawson, Hallett and Wilbourn: Entrapment Neuropathies
Preston and Shapiro: Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders
